topic: The political fight dominating August 3, 2026 is whether the Senate should cancel its August recess — or abolish the legislative filibuster — to force through the SAVE America Act, the proof-of-citizenship and photo-ID voting bill that has now failed on the Senate floor five times. The Senate returned Monday afternoon with four working days left before a recess scheduled to begin August 7, and with President Trump's demand hanging over the chamber: 'John Thune should not allow the United States Senate to "leave town" until it passes The Save America Act or, far better still, TERMINATES THE FILIBUSTER.' Sen. Mike Lee (R-Utah) has told the majority leader not to assume his consent to adjourn and has forced the question toward a roll-call vote; Sens. Rick Scott, Ashley Moody, Jim Banks and others have said they will vote to stay. Majority Leader John Thune has refused: 'We voted on it one, two, three, four, five times already,' he told reporters, and 'Show me how this ends. What's the picture of victory at the end?' — adding that when the White House met with roughly twenty Republican senators about ending the filibuster, 'There were 15 "noes."' The bill itself, S. 3752, is short and specific: a state 'shall not accept and process an application to register to vote in an election for Federal office unless the applicant presents documentary proof of United States citizenship,' and 'Each individual voting in an election for Federal office shall present an eligible photo identification document.' The House passed its version 218-213 on February 11, 2026. The checkable core is unusually well documented for an election-law fight: how much noncitizen voting actually occurs, how many citizens lack the documents, what the bill does and does not do, what happened in the states that already tried this, and whether the votes exist.
question: As of August 3, 2026, with four session days left before the August 7 recess, the argument is whether a national documentary-proof-of-citizenship and photo-ID requirement is a necessary fix to an unverifiable honor system or a solution in search of a problem that would cost eligible citizens their votes — and whether it is worth cancelling a recess or breaking the filibuster to get. Supporters — Trump, Sens. Mike Lee, Rick Scott, Ashley Moody, Jim Banks, Bill Hagerty, Tommy Tuberville, John Cornyn — answer that federal registration today rests on nothing but a signed attestation nobody checks, that a DHS review found roughly 278,000 noncitizens on state voter rolls, that 83 percent of Americans favor proving citizenship to register, and that the only reason to refuse is, in the President's words, that 'you want to cheat.' Opponents — every Senate Democrat, plus Republican Sens. Collins, Murkowski, McConnell and Tillis on the merits or the timing — answer that every serious audit and court finding puts noncitizen voting at a few dozen cases out of millions of ballots, that 21.3 million voting-age citizens lack ready access to a citizenship document, that Kansas's version of this law blocked 31,089 eligible applicants while catching 39 noncitizens, and that changing the rules three months before a midterm is the point rather than an accident. Which side's checkable claims hold up?
summary:
This is a fight where one side's central empirical claim is very well established and the other side's is not — but where the winning side's headline number is also inflated, and the losing side has two real points that its opponents mostly refuse to answer.

What verifies for the opponents. The rarity of noncitizen voting is not a partisan finding; it is the consistent result of every audit that has actually been completed, including audits run by Republicans. Georgia's Republican secretary of state audited 8.2 million registrations and found 20 noncitizens. A federal judge in Kansas, after a full trial, found 39 noncitizens on the rolls — 0.002 percent — and wrote that there was 'no iceberg; only an icicle, largely created by confusion and administrative error.' The Tenth Circuit affirmed unanimously. The same case establishes the cost side: Kansas's documentary-proof law blocked 31,089 applicants, 12.4 percent of new registrations, in three years. New Hampshire, which adopted a version of this in November 2024, turned away at least 244 would-be voters in 2025 by a voting-rights group's count, and a judge who reviewed the record there found that between 1998 and 2024 perhaps 8 of roughly 8.3 million votes cast may have involved noncitizens. Arizona currently has 43,385 people registered as 'federal only' voters because they never produced the document. And the pattern in every flagged-list episode is the same: initial numbers collapse on investigation — Iowa's 2,176 became 277; Denton County, Texas found that a quarter of its flagged voters had already shown proof of citizenship.

What verifies for the supporters. Three things, and they are not trivial. First, the honor-system point is simply true: 52 U.S.C. 20508(b)(2) requires the federal registration form to carry 'an attestation that the applicant meets each such requirement' signed 'under penalty of perjury,' and nothing more — there is no verification step, and states have no reliable citizenship database of their own. Second, the public agrees with them by a landslide: Gallup found 83 percent favor proving citizenship to register and 84 percent favor photo ID, including roughly 63 percent and 54 percent of Democrats. Third, the most-repeated attack on the bill — that it would stop married women who changed their names from voting — is overstated: the bill's text does direct states to let applicants 'provide such additional documentation' when documents don't match, though it leaves the process unspecified and pays for none of it. The 21.3 million figure is also softer than its usage: it comes from a 2,386-person survey commissioned by groups opposing the bill, it measures self-reported 'ready access' rather than possession, and the bill's registration requirement reaches new and re-registering voters rather than the existing rolls.

Where each side breaks. The supporters' factual case above the honor-system point does not survive contact with the record. Trump told the nation on July 16 that DHS 'identified approximately 278,000 non-citizens who are registered to vote in federal elections' and that 'the real number is actually much higher.' Pennsylvania's Republican secretary of state said his rolls are 'properly maintained' and that noncitizen voting is extremely rare; Nevada's called the numbers 'wildly speculative'; and a federal judge has already found the underlying DHS database was created unlawfully and 'used by some states to incorrectly remove U.S. citizens from their voter rolls.' The President's stated theory of the bill is also on the record and undercuts the integrity framing: at Mount Rushmore on July 4 he said that if the Senate terminates the filibuster and passes the bill, 'we will not lose an election for a hundred years.' The opponents break in the other direction: 'current safeguards are working' is an answer that never names what the safeguard is, and the honest description of the status quo is an unverified affidavit plus after-the-fact prosecution under 18 U.S.C. 611. And the filibuster argument is being made by senators who told Fox News last month they would eliminate it for their own voting bill.

What the meter cannot settle: how to trade a small number of illegitimate votes against a larger number of lost legitimate ones; whether elections belong to the states or to Congress; whether an unverifiable requirement is a defect even if nobody exploits it; and whether the filibuster is a safeguard or an obstruction. Note that the sharpest factual claims against the bill's prospects this week came from Republicans — Thune's vote count, Tillis's warning about changing rules months before an election.
verdict: On the checkable present-tense facts this leans toward the bill's opponents — leans, not sweeps, because their own headline number is soft and the supporters hold one point nobody has answered. What holds up against the bill is the empirical core: after Georgia's Republican-run audit of 8.2 million registrations found 20 noncitizens, after a federal trial in Kansas produced 39 out of 1.8 million and a judge's finding of 'no iceberg; only an icicle,' after New Hampshire's 8 possible noncitizen votes out of 8.3 million cast over 26 years, and after every flagged list from Iowa to Denton County shrank by an order of magnitude on investigation, the proposition that noncitizen registration is a material problem has been tested repeatedly and has not survived. The cost side is equally documented and comes from the same records: 31,089 Kansans blocked, 12.4 percent of new registrations; 43,385 Arizonans currently confined to federal-only ballots; at least 244 New Hampshire voters turned away in 2025. What does not hold up on the opponents' side is the way the burden is usually stated. '21.3 million disenfranchised' rests on a self-reported survey commissioned by the bill's opponents, measures 'ready access' rather than possession, and is applied to a requirement that by the bill's own terms governs applications 'submitted on or after' enactment rather than the existing rolls. The 'married women can't vote' line is likewise stronger in headlines than in the statute, which does instruct states to accept 'such additional documentation.' The supporters are scored lower because their load-bearing empirical claim is the one the record contradicts: the 278,000 figure the President announced from the White House is disputed by the Republican secretary of state of one of the four states named, rests on a database a federal judge found was unlawfully created and has already caused citizens to be wrongly removed, and follows the same trajectory as every prior claim of its kind. Their strongest point — that federal registration today verifies nothing beyond a signature under penalty of perjury, which is accurate as a matter of statute — is real, is largely unanswered by the other side, and is why this is not a rout. What the meter does not decide: whether one improper vote is worth more or less than one lost legitimate vote, whether Congress or the states should write election rules, or whether the filibuster should exist.

The Regulatory Review (academic, University of Pennsylvania) — 'Consequences of the SAVE America Act' (April 23, 2026; read directly): the bill would 'amend the National Voter Registration Act of 1993 to institute stricter requirements'; 'Over 21 million U.S. citizens lack immediate access to documents proving citizenship'; '2.6 million Americans do not possess government-issued photo IDs'; the revised bill passed the House in February 2026

Washington Times (right-leaning) — 'Senate to vote on stopgap bill to keep government open through Dec. 11' (August 2, 2026; read directly): the Senate's Monday test vote is on a continuing resolution extending fiscal 2026 levels ten weeks into fiscal 2027 to December 11, expected to clear 60 votes with bipartisan support; the article does not mention the SAVE America Act or the recess fight

left.label: We have run this experiment, and we know the answer. Kansas required documentary proof of citizenship for three years. A federal judge held a full trial and found 39 noncitizens on a roll of 1.8 million — 'no iceberg; only an icicle, largely created by confusion and administrative error' — while the law had blocked 31,089 eligible Kansans, 12.4 percent of everyone trying to register. The Tenth Circuit affirmed unanimously. Georgia's Republican secretary of state audited 8.2 million registrations and found 20 noncitizens. New Hampshire adopted this in 2024 and turned away at least 244 people last year; the judge who reviewed the record there found maybe 8 noncitizen votes out of 8.3 million cast since 1998 and wrote that noncitizen voting is 'essentially non-existent.' Arizona has 43,385 citizens stuck on federal-only ballots right now. Every dramatic number collapses when someone checks it: Iowa's 2,176 became 277; a quarter of the voters Texas flagged had already proved citizenship. And we know what this is for, because the President said it out loud at Mount Rushmore: pass it, and 'we will not lose an election for a hundred years.' You do not cancel a recess and break the Senate three months before a midterm to solve a problem measured in dozens.
left.framing: The opponents' empirical case is the strongest thing in this fight and it is not close: the rarity of noncitizen voting has been tested by Republican secretaries of state, by federal courts after trial, and by the Heritage Foundation's own database, and it comes back the same every time. The burden side is equally well documented and comes from the same litigation records rather than from advocacy estimates. Where the case weakens is in how the burden gets stated in public. '21.3 million disenfranchised' is a survey of self-reported 'ready access,' commissioned by groups opposing the bill, applied to a requirement the bill's own text limits to applications 'submitted on or after' enactment. The married-women line is stronger than the statute supports; the bill does instruct states to accept 'such additional documentation.' And 'current safeguards are working' is not an answer to the actual gap, which is that the safeguard is a signature. The strongest version of this case is not 'nobody is cheating' but 'the cure has a measured cost and the disease has a measured size, and they are three orders of magnitude apart.'
left.strongestPoint: The cost-benefit is not modeled; it has been measured, in court, under oath, by judges applying an evidentiary standard. In Fish v. Kobach the district court found after trial that Kansas's documentary-proof law had denied registration to '31,089 total applicants,' 12.4 percent of new registrations over three years, while producing 39 noncitizen registrants — '0.002% of all registered voters in Kansas' — and Judge Robinson wrote that there was 'no iceberg; only an icicle, largely created by confusion and administrative error.' The Tenth Circuit affirmed unanimously in 2020. New Hampshire's version produced the same ratio from the other direction: a judge reviewing that record in May 2026 found perhaps 8 of roughly 8.3 million votes cast between 1998 and 2024 may have involved noncitizens and concluded that 'wrongful voting by noncitizens is essentially non-existent,' while a voting-rights group counted at least 244 people turned away in 2025 alone. Georgia's Republican secretary of state found 20 noncitizens in 8.2 million registrations. Arizona currently has 43,385 people confined to federal-only ballots. Every one of these numbers comes from a state that actually tried the policy.
left.weakestPoint: The headline numbers are inflated in exactly the way the other side says they are. The 21.3 million figure is a 2,386-person SSRS survey of self-reported 'ready access to a document proving citizenship' — not possession, not a registration outcome — fielded in fall 2023 and commissioned by VoteRiders, the Brennan Center and the University of Maryland, all of which oppose the bill; PBS's phrasing that the bill 'could disenfranchise approximately 20 million American voters' treats a survey response as a lost vote. It also elides what the bill actually reaches: by its own terms the registration requirement 'shall apply with respect to applications for voter registration which are submitted on or after' enactment, so it governs new and re-registering voters, not the existing rolls. Rep. Scholten's claim that 167,000 women in her district 'could find themselves unable to register' runs past a provision directing states to let applicants 'provide such additional documentation.' And Sen. Padilla's 'current safeguards are working' never names the safeguard, which is an attestation 'under penalty of perjury' with no verification behind it. The filibuster argument is also newly acquired: Sens. Blumenthal and Cantwell told Fox News last month they favor eliminating it for measures they want, Cantwell saying 'When we wanted the Voting Rights Act passed, I was willing to do it.'
left.unknowns: How many of the 21.3 million would actually fail to register under this bill is unknown; the survey measures a self-reported condition rather than a registration outcome, and the state-level natural experiments (Kansas 12.4 percent of applicants, New Hampshire's 244) suggest a real but much smaller number that no one has projected nationally. Whether the states' name-discrepancy processes would be workable is unknown because the bill does not specify them and appropriates nothing for them; the reconciliation vehicle's $10 billion would change that calculation but has not passed. Whether the Supreme Court's pending Arizona case will change what Congress may require of the federal form is unknown and will not be decided before the midterms. And whether Trump's Mount Rushmore statement about not losing 'an election for a hundred years' reflects a modeled expectation or is rhetoric cannot be determined from the record.

right.label: Right now, a person registers to vote in a federal election by checking a box and signing a form. That is the whole verification system — 52 U.S.C. 20508 requires 'an attestation that the applicant meets each such requirement' signed 'under penalty of perjury,' and it specifically forbids requiring notarization or any other authentication. No state has a citizenship database it can check against. When DHS finally ran the rolls of four states that refuse to cooperate, it found roughly 278,000 people who appear to be noncitizens registered to vote, and agencies in Texas have been caught registering people who told them outright they were not citizens. Eighty-three percent of Americans — including 63 percent of Democrats — think you should have to prove citizenship the first time you register, and 84 percent want photo ID. The bill does not touch anyone already registered, and it instructs states to create a process for people whose documents show a different name. There is no honest objection left. The Senate has a Republican majority, four days before it leaves town, and one procedural rule standing between the American people and something they overwhelmingly want.
right.framing: The supporters hold one point that the other side has not answered and mostly does not engage: federal registration verifies nothing. The statute is explicit that the form carries an attestation under penalty of perjury and 'may not include any requirement for notarization or other formal authentication,' and the enforcement mechanism is a criminal statute applied after the fact. That is a genuine structural gap, and 83 percent public support for closing it is real and cross-partisan. Two other supporting claims are also correct and routinely misstated by critics: the registration requirement reaches applications submitted after enactment rather than the existing rolls, and the bill does direct states to accept 'such additional documentation' for name discrepancies. What sinks the score is the empirical claim the campaign is actually built on. The 278,000 figure was announced from the White House without a published methodology, is disputed by the Republican secretary of state of one of the four states named, rests on a database a federal judge found was created unlawfully and has already caused citizens to be wrongly purged, and follows the identical trajectory of Iowa's 2,176-to-277 and Texas's flagged-list collapse. And the President's own account of the bill's purpose — 'we will not lose an election for a hundred years' — is a candid statement of electoral advantage that the integrity framing cannot absorb.
right.strongestPoint: The status quo verifies nothing, and this is a matter of statutory text rather than argument. 52 U.S.C. 20508(b)(2) requires the federal mail registration form to contain a statement that 'specifies each eligibility requirement (including citizenship),' 'contains an attestation that the applicant meets each such requirement,' and 'requires the signature of the applicant, under penalty of perjury' — and subsection (b)(3) provides that it 'may not include any requirement for notarization or other formal authentication.' There is no verification step in federal law, and states have no independent citizenship database; the only backstop is prosecution under 18 U.S.C. 611 after the vote has already been counted. That agencies do erroneously register noncitizens is documented by a source hostile to the claim's political use: the Center for Election Innovation and Research found that in Denton County, Texas, 14 of 84 flagged records were 'self-identified noncitizens mistakenly registered by agencies.' And the public's view is not close and not partisan: Gallup found 83 percent favor proving citizenship at first registration and 84 percent favor photo ID, with roughly 63 percent and 54 percent of Democrats agreeing, on 1,023 adults with a ±4-point margin. Two of the loudest attacks on the bill are also overstated against its text: it applies to applications 'submitted on or after' enactment, and it directs states to let applicants 'provide such additional documentation' when names do not match.
right.weakestPoint: The campaign's central factual claim is the one the record most consistently contradicts, and the President said the quiet part on camera. On July 16 he told the nation that DHS 'identified approximately 278,000 non-citizens who are registered to vote in federal elections' and that 'the real number is actually much higher than that.' Pennsylvania's Republican Secretary of State Al Schmidt said his rolls are 'properly maintained and updated' and that noncitizen voting is 'extremely rare'; Nevada's secretary said the numbers were 'wildly speculative at best'; a federal judge has found the SAVE database was created unlawfully and 'used by some states to incorrectly remove U.S. citizens from their voter rolls.' Every prior list of this kind has collapsed on investigation — Iowa's 2,176 to 277, Michigan's to 16 out of 5.7 million votes, and in Denton County 37 of 84 flagged voters had already shown proof of citizenship. The reasoning problem is separate and larger: 'The only reason you wouldn't do it is you want to cheat' is not an argument, and at Mount Rushmore on July 4 the President described the payoff as 'if we terminate the filibuster as we should do and immediately vote for the SAVE America Act, then we will not lose an election for a hundred years.' The White House campaign page also advertises limiting mail voting to 'Illness, Disability, Military or Travel,' which appears nowhere in S. 3752's three sections. And the procedural demand is new: Sen. Cornyn wrote on March 11, 2026 that 'For many years, I believed that if the U.S. Senate scrapped the filibuster, Texas and our nation would stand to lose more than we would gain,' before endorsing 'whatever changes to Senate rules that may prove necessary.'
right.unknowns: Whether any part of the 278,000 figure survives investigation is unknown; DHS has not published its methodology, the four states named have not been given the underlying records by their own accounts, and no state has completed a verification of the flagged names. Whether the SAVE database's error rate is small enough to use for removals is unknown and is the subject of active litigation. Whether the bill would in fact prevent any noncitizen from registering — as opposed to shifting the error from registration to document verification — has not been estimated by any nonpartisan body. And whether Republicans could pass the bill even without the filibuster is genuinely uncertain: the June 4, 2026 attempt to attach it to an immigration package failed 48-50 with four Republicans voting no, meaning it did not command a simple majority.

facts.claim: The SAVE America Act would bar states from processing a federal voter registration application without documentary proof of citizenship, and would require photo identification to vote in federal elections.
facts.evidence: S. 3752, 119th Congress, introduced text (primary, read in full at govinfo.gov): 'the State shall not accept and process an application to register to vote in an election for Federal office unless the applicant presents documentary proof of United States citizenship'; 'Each individual voting in an election for Federal office shall present an eligible photo identification document'; for absentee voters, 'the individual shall include a copy of the eligible photo identification document-- (A) with the request for an absentee ballot; and (B) with the submission of the absentee ballot'; and the effective-date clause provides it 'shall apply with respect to applications for voter registration which are submitted on or after such date.'
facts.explanation: Graded on the bill text itself, which is why no corroboration is required and confidence is high. Three details matter and are routinely lost in coverage. First, the bill has exactly three sections — short title, registration, photo ID — and contains no provision eliminating or curtailing mail voting beyond requiring an ID copy with the request and the returned ballot. Second, the registration requirement by its own terms governs applications submitted after enactment, so it reaches new and re-registering voters rather than the existing rolls; FactCheck.org confirms this reading. Third, the bill creates new criminal exposure and an expanded private right of action reaching 'the act of an election official who registers an applicant to vote in an election for Federal office who fails to present documentary proof of United States citizenship,' a provision the National Association of Counties flags as a burden on local administrators. The House version passed 218-213 on February 11, 2026.
facts.source: S. 3752 — SAVE America Act, introduced text (primary)

corroboration.source: FactCheck.org (nonpartisan) — Q&A on the SAVE America Act (confirming the text and that it reaches reregistration rather than all current voters)
National Association of Counties (nonpartisan) — House passes SAVE America Act; Major impacts on county election administration (the 218-213 February 11, 2026 vote and the administrative burdens)

facts.claim: Documented noncitizen voting and registration in U.S. elections is extremely rare — on the order of tens of cases against millions of ballots.
facts.evidence: Fish v. Kobach: the district court found after trial that only 39 noncitizens had successfully registered in Kansas, '0.002% of all registered voters,' and Judge Julie Robinson wrote there was 'no iceberg; only an icicle, largely created by confusion and administrative error'; the Tenth Circuit affirmed unanimously on April 29, 2020. PBS NewsHour (read directly): a judge reviewing New Hampshire's record in May 2026 found that between 1998 and 2024 only 8 of roughly 8.3 million votes cast may have involved noncitizens and wrote, 'If wrongful voting is rare in New Hampshire, wrongful voting by noncitizens is essentially non-existent.' FactCheck.org (read directly): Georgia's audit found 20 noncitizens out of 8.2 million registered voters, nine of whom had voted; the Heritage Foundation's own database records 'only 77 instances of noncitizen voting between 1999-2023.' Brennan Center (read directly): officials overseeing '23.5 million votes in the 2016 election referred only about 30 incidents of suspected noncitizen voting ... That is .0001 percent.'
facts.explanation: This is graded supported at high confidence because the finding is replicated across sources with opposite political interests: a federal court after adversarial trial, a Republican secretary of state's own audit, a conservative think tank's own database, and a left-leaning research center. The Cato Institute's Walter Olson, quoted by FactCheck.org, states the conservative version: 'the number of noncitizens illegally voting in federal elections is extremely low, not high enough to have changed the party outcome of any federal election in recent years.' Two honest caveats. Detection is imperfect — audits find what their matching methods can find, and a determined noncitizen voter who never encounters an immigration database would not appear in these counts, so 'documented' is doing real work in the claim. And 'rare' is not 'zero': Louisiana reported 403 flagged noncitizens with 83 having voted, Utah confirmed 27, and Ohio indicted six for voting between 2008 and 2020. The distinction that matters is order of magnitude, and on that the record is consistent.
facts.source: PBS NewsHour — Judge says New Hampshire must loosen proof-of-citizenship rules for voter registration (the court's findings on New Hampshire's rate)

corroboration.source: FactCheck.org (nonpartisan) — Q&A on the SAVE America Act (Georgia's 20 of 8.2 million; Heritage Foundation's 77 instances; Cato's Walter Olson)
Fish v. Kobach — case record of the district court and Tenth Circuit findings ('no iceberg; only an icicle')
Brennan Center for Justice (left-leaning) — Noncitizen Voting is Vanishingly Rare (the 2016 figure of ~30 referrals out of 23.5 million votes)

facts.claim: A Department of Homeland Security review identified approximately 278,000 noncitizens registered to vote, including more than 250,000 in California, New Jersey, Nevada and Pennsylvania.
facts.evidence: President Trump, Address to the Nation on Election Security, July 16, 2026 (primary transcript, read at the Miller Center): 'According to the DHS review, state voter rolls, and public records, they identified approximately 278,000 non-citizens who are registered to vote in federal elections,' and 'Since Democrat states refuse to share their voter files, the real number is actually much higher than that.' CBS News (read directly): the DHS preliminary figures were 190,832 for California, 35,152 for New Jersey, 15,903 for Nevada and 14,576 for Pennsylvania; Pennsylvania's Republican Secretary of State Al Schmidt said the state's rolls are 'properly maintained and updated' and that noncitizen voting is 'extremely rare'; Nevada's Francisco Aguilar: 'These numbers are wildly speculative at best and the Department of Homeland Security hasn't shared anything that backs it up'; election expert David Becker: the 'data includes a ton of people, maybe even a majority of people, who are absolutely eligible voters'; a federal judge found the administration 'acted unlawfully' creating the database and that it had been 'used by some states to incorrectly remove U.S. citizens from their voter rolls.'
facts.explanation: Graded mostly-false rather than false because the underlying DHS matching exercise is real and produced these raw counts — the figures are not invented. What is false is the characterization: these are unverified flags, not identified noncitizens, and the President presented them as the latter and then said the true number is higher. Three things establish the grade. First, the rebuttal is cross-partisan: the Republican secretary of state of one of the four states named contradicts the claim about his own rolls, which is the strongest form of corroboration available. Second, the flagged-versus-confirmed gap has been measured repeatedly and is enormous: the Center for Election Innovation and Research documents Iowa's October 2024 claim of 2,176 falling to 277 confirmed by March 2025, Michigan's confirmed total of 16 out of roughly 5.7 million votes cast, and Denton County, Texas, where 37 of 84 SAVE-flagged records belonged to people who had already shown proof of citizenship at registration. Third, USCIS itself acknowledges 'gaps in the data available to SAVE.' Confidence is medium rather than high because DHS has published no methodology at all — meaning the claim cannot be conclusively falsified either, only shown to be of a type that has never held up. Note the internal tension in the President's own framing: three of the four states he names as withholding files are the states DHS says it reviewed from public records.
facts.source: Miller Center — transcript of President Trump's July 16, 2026 Address to the Nation on Election Security (primary)

corroboration.source: CBS News — What to know about the Trump administration's claim that 250K noncitizens are registered to vote in 4 states (the state-by-state figures and the officials' rebuttals, including Pennsylvania's Republican secretary of state)
Center for Election Innovation and Research (nonpartisan) — Update: Review of Claims of Noncitizen Registrants and Voters (the flagged-to-confirmed collapse in Iowa, Michigan and Texas)
The Federalist (right-leaning) — DHS: Over 250K Noncitizens Are Registered To Vote In Four States (the claim as made, with no methodology stated)

facts.claim: Federal law currently verifies citizenship at registration only through a signed attestation under penalty of perjury, and forbids requiring any further authentication on the federal form.
facts.evidence: 52 U.S.C. 20508(b) (primary, read at Cornell's Legal Information Institute): the federal mail voter registration form must include a statement that '(A) specifies each eligibility requirement (including citizenship); (B) contains an attestation that the applicant meets each such requirement; and (C) requires the signature of the applicant, under penalty of perjury'; and subsection (b)(3) provides that the form 'may not include any requirement for notarization or other formal authentication.' 18 U.S.C. 611(a)-(b) (primary, same source): 'It shall be unlawful for any alien to vote in any election held solely or in part for the purpose of electing a candidate for the office of President, Vice President ... Member of the Senate, Member of the House of Representatives'; 'Any person who violates this section shall be fined under this title, imprisoned not more than one year, or both.'
facts.explanation: This is the supporters' strongest claim and it is graded on the statutes themselves. The federal registration system takes an applicant's word, and the sole federal enforcement mechanism operates after the fact through criminal prosecution. Two caveats keep this from carrying more weight than it does. First, 'unverified' is not the same as 'unverifiable in practice': states run list-maintenance programs under 52 U.S.C. 20507, jury-duty and DMV records surface noncitizens, and voting is a deportable offense — which is a large part of why the measured rate is so low. Second, the honor system's failure mode in the documented cases is usually administrative rather than fraudulent: the Center for Election Innovation and Research found that in Denton County, Texas, the noncitizens on the rolls were people who had told an agency they were not citizens and were registered anyway. That is a real defect and it argues for something; whether it argues for this bill is a policy judgment the meter does not make. What the meter records is that critics who answer this point with 'current safeguards are working' are not describing what the safeguard is.
facts.source: 52 U.S.C. 20508 — National Voter Registration Act, contents of the federal mail registration form (primary)

corroboration.source: 18 U.S.C. 611 — Voting by aliens (primary; the after-the-fact criminal enforcement mechanism)
Center for Election Innovation and Research (nonpartisan) — Denton County, Texas: 14 of 84 flagged records were self-identified noncitizens mistakenly registered by agencies

facts.claim: Roughly 21.3 million voting-age U.S. citizens — 9.1 percent — lack ready access to documentary proof of citizenship, and the SAVE America Act would therefore disenfranchise about 20 million Americans.
facts.evidence: Brennan Center for Justice (read directly): '9.1 percent of American citizens of voting age, or 21.3 million people, lack ready access to a document proving citizenship,' with at least 3.8 million lacking them entirely; an SSRS survey of '2,386 U.S. citizens age 18 and older' fielded in fall 2023 for VoteRiders, the University of Maryland's Center for Democracy and Civic Engagement and the Brennan Center; the page states no margin of error and notes the survey 'didn't cover the reasons why.' PBS NewsHour (read directly): 'Voting experts estimate the bill could disenfranchise approximately 20 million American voters lacking readily available documentation.' Against that framing, S. 3752's own text: the requirement 'shall apply with respect to applications for voter registration which are submitted on or after' enactment. FactCheck.org (read directly): the requirement applies when voters register or reregister after moving or a name change, 'not all current voters.'
facts.explanation: Graded mixed because the underlying survey finding is real and reasonably reported while the inference drawn from it in political usage is not supportable. Three problems with the '20 million disenfranchised' framing, all of which the other side names correctly. The survey measures self-reported 'ready access,' not possession and not a registration outcome — a citizen whose birth certificate is in a filing cabinet at their parents' house is in the 21.3 million and would not lose a vote. It was commissioned by three organizations that oppose the bill, which is disclosed but is a provenance caveat. And it is applied to a requirement that by the statute's terms governs new and re-registering applicants rather than the 160-odd million people already on the rolls. The Bipartisan Policy Center's independent estimate — that about 12 percent of registered voters lack the documentation the act specifies — is in the same range and comes from MIT survey data, which is why the underlying condition is not in dispute. The measured real-world rate is the better guide and is smaller but far from trivial: Kansas blocked 12.4 percent of new registrants; New Hampshire turned away at least 244 people in 2025; Arizona has 43,385 federal-only voters. Confidence medium: survey-based, sponsor-aligned, and no page I could read gave a margin of error.
facts.source: Brennan Center for Justice (left-leaning) — 21.3 Million American Citizens of Voting Age Don't Have Ready Access to Citizenship Documents

corroboration.source: Bipartisan Policy Center (centrist) — Six Things to Know About the SAVE America Act (independent 12-percent estimate from MIT survey data; the 21.3 million figure attributed to the University of Maryland center)
FactCheck.org (nonpartisan) — Q&A on the SAVE America Act (that the requirement applies on registration and reregistration, not to all current voters)

facts.claim: Where documentary proof of citizenship has actually been imposed, it has blocked large numbers of eligible citizens from registering or voting.
facts.evidence: Fish v. Kobach: the court found '31,089 total applicants ... were denied registration for failure to provide DPOC' between January 1, 2013 and December 11, 2015, '12.4% of new voter registrations,' and the Tenth Circuit affirmed unanimously on April 29, 2020, finding the law had 'an undue impact by cancelling or suspending the voter registrations of 31,089 voters.' Bipartisan Policy Center (read directly, centrist): the Kansas law 'prevented roughly 31,000 eligible citizens, or 12% of all applicants, from registering to vote.' Arizona Capitol Times (read directly): '43,385 registered voters are currently permitted to vote only in federal elections' because they did not provide documentary proof. New Hampshire Bulletin via Yahoo reprint (read directly): 'According to a tally by the New Hampshire Campaign for Voting Rights, 123 voters were turned away from the polls due to a lack of documents' at October and November 2025 municipal elections, plus 121 at spring town meetings, 'at least 244 people' in 2025.
facts.explanation: Graded supported at high confidence because the two largest figures come from judicial findings after adversarial proceedings and are corroborated by a centrist think tank, and the Arizona figure comes from the state's own bifurcated registration system as reported in coverage of the Supreme Court's June 29, 2026 cert grant. The New Hampshire tally is the weakest link in the chain and is flagged as such: it was compiled by an advocacy group, the state has not published a competing count, and 'turned away' includes people who returned later with documents — Votebeat's reporting describes voters making two and three trips. The strongest contrary point, which supporters make fairly, is that Kansas's implementation was unusually chaotic and that a funded, well-designed system with a working cure process would perform better; the SAVE America Act appropriates nothing, though the House reconciliation vehicle would provide $10 billion. Note also that Kansas and Arizona were state-imposed requirements struck down or limited under the NVRA, whereas Congress acting under the Elections Clause would not face the same preemption problem — the burden evidence transfers, the legal posture does not.
facts.source: Fish v. Kobach — case record of the district court and Tenth Circuit findings (31,089 applicants denied; 12.4 percent of new registrations)

corroboration.source: Bipartisan Policy Center (centrist) — Six Things to Know About the SAVE America Act (roughly 31,000 eligible citizens, 12 percent of applicants)
Arizona Capitol Times — US Supreme Court to review Arizona's 'proof of citizenship' voter law (43,385 federal-only voters)
New Hampshire Bulletin via Yahoo reprint — After 123 voters turned away at municipal elections, advocates criticize proof-of-citizenship law

facts.claim: Large majorities of Americans, including most Democrats, support requiring proof of citizenship to register and photo identification to vote.
facts.evidence: Gallup, 'Americans Endorse Both Early Voting and Voter Verification' (read directly): '84%' of U.S. adults favor requiring photo identification to vote and '83%' favor providing proof of citizenship when registering to vote for the first time; Democrats support photo ID at 54 percent and proof of citizenship at roughly 63 percent, Republicans at 84 and roughly 93 percent; '1,023 adults, aged 18 and older,' interviewed 'Oct. 1-12, 2024,' margin of error '±4 percentage points at the 95% confidence level.'
facts.explanation: Graded supported at high confidence on a directly read poll from a nonpartisan firm with full methodology disclosed. Two caveats that matter for how the number is used. The question asked is about the principle — proof of citizenship at first registration, photo ID at the polls — not about this bill, which requires documentary proof presented in person, restricts the acceptable document set to exclude an ordinary driver's license, and attaches criminal exposure for election officials. Support for a principle routinely exceeds support for a specific implementation, and the Gallup wording does not test the implementation. Second, the poll is from October 2024 and Gallup notes results similar to July 2022, so the reading is stable but nearly two years old as of this fight. What it does establish, and what critics who call the bill purely a suppression scheme have to reckon with, is that a majority of Democratic voters agree with the underlying requirement.
facts.source: Gallup — Americans Endorse Both Early Voting and Voter Verification

facts.claim: The SAVE America Act would prevent married women who changed their surname from registering to vote, because their birth certificates carry a different name.
facts.evidence: Rep. Hillary Scholten, quoted in Fox News (read directly): 'Nearly 70 million married women in this country have changed their last name, but their birth certificates don't reflect that,' and 167,000 women in her district 'could find themselves unable to register.' Against it, S. 3752's own text (primary, read at govinfo.gov): the bill establishes a process for applicants to 'provide such additional documentation' where documents do not match; Rep. Lance Gooden said the bill 'directs states to create a process to address discrepancies with name changes' and called the claim 'a fallacy intended to fearmonger.' FactCheck.org (read directly), quoting VoteRiders legal director Ceridwen Cherry: 'If a voter has experienced a name change they would not be able to use their birth certificate as their only proof of citizenship as this document does not get updated if someone changes their name through marriage or divorce,' while noting the bill requires states to establish accommodating processes 'though specific requirements remain unspecified.'
facts.explanation: Graded mixed because the underlying mismatch is real and the conclusion drawn from it is overstated. What is true: a birth certificate alone will not satisfy the requirement for someone whose legal name has changed, so those voters need a linking document — a marriage certificate or a court order — in addition. What is not established: that they would be 'unable to register.' The bill's text directs states to accept additional documentation, and a Federalist Society analysis cited by Fox News notes the Election Assistance Commission is directed to issue guidelines for supplementary documents such as a marriage license. The honest version of the critics' point is about friction and cost rather than prohibition, and New Hampshire supplies the concrete illustration: Votebeat reported a Derry voter sent home once for her birth certificate and a second time for her marriage certificate. Confidence is medium because the bill leaves the cure process to states without specifying or funding it, so how burdensome it would be in practice is genuinely unknown and depends entirely on implementation. Note that the 70 million figure describes people who have changed their surname, not people who would fail to register.
facts.source: Fox News (right-leaning) — Democrat claims SAVE Act would block married women from voting, Republicans say that's wrong

corroboration.source: S. 3752 — SAVE America Act, introduced text (primary; the 'such additional documentation' provision)
FactCheck.org (nonpartisan) — Q&A on the SAVE America Act (the mismatch is real; the state cure processes are unspecified)

facts.claim: Senate Republicans do not have the votes to pass the SAVE America Act or to abolish the filibuster, whether or not the August recess is cancelled.
facts.evidence: Washington Examiner (right-leaning, read directly): Thune said the White House met with 20 Republican senators about ending the filibuster and 'There were 15 "noes."' PBS NewsHour (read directly): Thune, 'We voted on it one, two, three, four, five times already,' and 'Show me how this ends. What's the picture of victory at the end?' powerLens.thesis: The power test on this issue is close to a controlled experiment, because the roles were reversed almost exactly four years ago and the same institution was the battlefield. In January 2022 a Democratic president and a Democratic Senate majority demanded that the legislative filibuster be carved out so that Congress could pass a federal election law — the Freedom to Vote Act and the John Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act — over unanimous Republican objection, on the theory that the stakes for democracy were too high for a procedural rule to stand in the way. The Senate rejected the rules change 52-48 on January 19, 2022, with Sens. Manchin and Sinema joining every Republican. Republicans, John Thune foremost among them, called it an attempt to force through 'a federal election takeover to give his party an advantage in future elections.' In August 2026 the identical demand is being made by a Republican president and a Republican Senate majority for a federal election law of their own, and Thune is again the man refusing — the rare figure whose position did not move. Almost everyone else's did. Sen. John Cornyn wrote in March that he had believed for years that scrapping the filibuster would cost Texas more than it gained, then endorsed 'whatever changes to Senate rules that may prove necessary' to pass this bill. On the other side, Sens. Blumenthal and Cantwell told Fox News last month that they favor eliminating the filibuster for the measures they want, Cantwell saying flatly, 'When we wanted the Voting Rights Act passed, I was willing to do it.' None of this decides who is right about noncitizen voting rates, document access or what the bill's text says, and the needle does not move on it.

precedent.case: The January 2022 Senate fight over carving out the legislative filibuster to pass the Freedom to Vote Act and the John Lewis Voting Rights Advancement Act.
precedent.what: President Biden, in a January 2022 speech in Atlanta, called for changing Senate rules to pass federal voting legislation; Majority Leader Schumer forced the question. On January 19, 2022, the Senate first failed to break a Republican filibuster of the combined voting bill, then rejected a 'talking filibuster' rules change 52-48, with Democrats Joe Manchin and Kyrsten Sinema joining all 50 Republicans. Republicans framed the effort as a partisan power grab dressed as democracy protection. Thune, then the Republican whip, said on the floor that Democrats were 'undermining the filibuster in hopes of forcing through a federal election takeover to give his party an advantage in future elections,' adding, 'that is what we are talking about, federalizing elections in this country.' He had earlier called the For the People Act 'an unacceptable federal takeover of elections.'
precedent.mirror: Swap the party labels and August 2026 is the same tableau. A president demands the Senate break its own rule to pass a national election statute his party wrote and the other party unanimously opposes; the majority leader says the votes are not there; the president's allies threaten to block adjournment; and the out-party discovers the virtues of the sixty-vote threshold. The mapping is not perfect, and the differences cut both ways. The 2022 bills would have expanded access and the 2026 bill restricts it, which is the substantive difference that matters most to partisans and least to the procedural question. And the Elections Clause argument the Republicans lost in 2022 — that Congress federalizing state election administration is illegitimate — is now the argument the Republicans need, since Article I, Section 4 provides that 'Congress may at any time by Law make or alter such Regulations.' Congress does have the power. That was true in 2022 and it is true now. The stable element is institutional rather than partisan: the filibuster is a principle to whichever party is one vote short of a majority's ambitions, and an obstruction to whichever party has the majority.

flips.then: From 2021 through 2022, Republicans made two arguments in tandem: that the legislative filibuster is a constitutional safeguard that a majority must not break for partisan advantage, and that Congress writing national rules for state-run elections is an illegitimate 'federal takeover.' Thune's own formulation on the Senate floor in January 2022 — quoted from a search-indexed copy of his press release, which thune.senate.gov would not serve directly — was that Democrats were 'undermining the filibuster in hopes of forcing through a federal election takeover to give his party an advantage in future elections.' Sen. John Cornyn put the filibuster half in writing: 'For many years, I believed that if the U.S. Senate scrapped the filibuster, Texas and our nation would stand to lose more than we would gain.'
flips.now: In 2026 the President demands the filibuster be terminated to pass a national election statute — 'far better still, TERMINATES THE FILIBUSTER, where Republicans can then quickly pass everything they ever dreamed of' — and states the expected partisan payoff explicitly, telling a Mount Rushmore audience on July 4 that if the Senate does it and passes the bill, 'we will not lose an election for a hundred years.' Cornyn reversed on March 11, 2026: 'I support whatever changes to Senate rules that may prove necessary for us to get the SAVE America Act ... past the Democrats' obstruction,' explaining that 'when the reality on the ground changes, leaders must take stock and adapt.' The 'federal takeover' objection has disappeared entirely from the Republican case, since the bill is a federal mandate on all fifty states. The consistent exceptions, applying the same standard under both presidents, are Thune, who is refusing, and Sens. Collins, Murkowski, McConnell and Tillis, who voted against attaching the bill to a reconciliation package on June 4.

flips.then: In January 2022, Senate Democrats voted 48-52 to change the filibuster rules specifically so a bare majority could pass a federal election law over unanimous minority objection, and argued that a procedural rule could not be permitted to block legislation about democracy itself. Schumer's framing ahead of the vote was 'Tonight let us sidestep voting rights no more.' As recently as 2024 he told reporters that with Manchin and Sinema gone the votes for a carve-out were there: 'Ruben Gallego is for it, and we have 51.'
flips.now: In 2026 Senate Democrats are the filibuster's beneficiaries and defenders on this bill, and several have said out loud that the principle is conditional. Sen. Angela Alsobrooks: 'I think we have to be really careful. The filibuster is what's preventing President Trump from his SAVE Act.' Sen. Richard Blumenthal: 'I'm in favor of eliminating the filibuster for specific measures, not across the board.' Sen. Maria Cantwell, asked whether she would end it: 'When we wanted the Voting Rights Act passed, I was willing to do it.' That is a candid statement of a position that turns on the contents of the bill rather than on the rule, which is the same position Republicans held in reverse in 2022 — and it is why Democrats earn no reasoning-honesty credit here for institutionalism. Their substantive case against the bill stands on its own evidence and does not depend on the procedural argument.

powerLens.longRun: Strip out who holds the Senate and a durable structure appears. The Elections Clause gives Congress plenary authority to 'make or alter' the rules for federal elections, so the constitutional question in these fights is almost never whether Congress may act — it is whether sixty senators will let it. That means every generation's election-law ambition, in either direction, dies at the same procedural checkpoint, and every party that reaches that checkpoint discovers the same argument: that this particular bill is too important for the rule. The Freedom to Vote Act died there in 2022; the SAVE America Act has died there five times since March 2026. The second durable feature is the ratio at the center of this dispute. Every serious audit ever conducted has found documented noncitizen voting in the range of tens to low hundreds against millions of ballots, and every documentary-proof requirement ever imposed has blocked eligible citizens in the thousands to tens of thousands. Those two facts have been stable across Republican and Democratic administrations, in red states and blue, since Arizona's Proposition 200 in 2004, and nothing in the current fight has changed either one. The prediction when power changes hands is straightforward. A Democratic Senate majority will introduce a national voting-access bill; Republicans will call it a federal takeover and filibuster it; Democrats will demand a carve-out; and the senators who spent August 2026 arguing that a single procedural rule must not be allowed to stand between the people and their preference will discover that it is the last bulwark of the republic.
powerLens.appliedToScore: The power test docks reasoning honesty on both sides and hands neither a consistency bonus. The Republican side earns no reasoning credit for the proposition that Congress must act nationally on elections, having spent 2021 and 2022 arguing that exactly this is illegitimate, and none for the urgency of breaking the filibuster, having defended it as a constitutional safeguard when the shoe was on the other foot; Cornyn's reversal is in his own writing and is recorded in the side's weakest point. The Democratic side earns no reasoning credit for institutional defense of the filibuster, because three of its own senators have said in the past month that they would eliminate it for bills they favor. Both deductions are already priced into the reasoning-honesty scores above. The needle rests on present-tense checkables and nothing else: what the bill's text actually requires (documentary proof at registration and photo ID at voting, applying to applications submitted after enactment, with a state-run cure process for name mismatches); what current law requires (an attestation under penalty of perjury with no authentication permitted on the federal form); how much noncitizen voting audits actually find (tens to low hundreds against millions); whether the 278,000 figure has been substantiated (no, and disputed by a Republican secretary of state among the four states named); how many eligible citizens documentary-proof laws have blocked where tried (31,089 in Kansas, 43,385 currently in Arizona, at least 244 in New Hampshire in 2025); what the public wants (83 to 84 percent support in principle); and whether the votes exist (they do not, by the majority leader's count and two failed floor votes). On that ledger the bill's opponents are right about more of the load-bearing facts and wrong about the size of their headline number; the bill's supporters are right about the honor-system gap and the public's view and wrong about the scale of the problem. That is a lean, not a rout.
powerLens.unknowns: The power test scores consistency, not correctness, and the 2022 and 2026 bills are not equivalent in kind — one expanded access and the other conditions it, which is a substantive difference the procedural symmetry cannot capture. Whether the senators applying a consistent standard now would do so if their own party's bill were on the floor cannot be tested, and Thune's consistency is confounded by his institutional role as the leader who would have to execute the rules change. pattern.thesis: Treating the recess fight as a discrete procedural dispute about one bill keeps the argument off the trajectory it belongs to, and that is the frame both sides find convenient — supporters because it makes the question 'why won't Thune schedule a vote,' opponents because it makes the question 'why is Trump bullying the Senate.' The SAVE America Act is the legislative arm of a three-year, multi-track effort to impose documentary proof of citizenship on federal elections: by executive order, by federal database, by litigation, by state law, and by statute. Each track has been tried, most have been checked by courts, and the legislative track is the one that survives judicial review if it ever passes, which is why it is the one being pressed hardest three months before a midterm. The instances below are not offered as evidence that any of them is illegitimate — Congress plainly has Elections Clause authority to legislate here, and 83 percent of the public supports the underlying principle. They are offered because the recurring question is the same in every instance and has been answered the same way every time: when a citizenship-verification mechanism is actually tested against records, the number of noncitizens it finds is small and the number of citizens it burdens is larger.

campaigns.where: 2004-2020 — Arizona's Proposition 200 and Kansas's documentary-proof law
campaigns.what: Arizona voters approved Proposition 200 in 2004 requiring documentary proof of citizenship to register; the Supreme Court held in 2013 that the NVRA preempts the requirement for the federal form, producing Arizona's bifurcated system, which today has 43,385 'federal only' voters. Kansas enacted a similar law in 2013; after a full trial, a federal court found it had denied registration to 31,089 applicants — 12.4 percent of new registrations — while producing 39 noncitizen registrants, 0.002 percent of the roll, and Judge Robinson wrote that there was 'no iceberg; only an icicle.' The Tenth Circuit affirmed unanimously in 2020.
campaigns.authorization: Struck down / limited by federal courts under the NVRA and the Equal Protection Clause

campaigns.what: New Hampshire's 2024 law required hard-copy citizenship documents for first-time registrants and eliminated the qualified-voter affidavit that had allowed election-day registrants to attest to citizenship under penalty of perjury. A voting-rights group counted at least 244 people turned away in 2025. pattern.takeaway: The recurring question across all five instances is not whether Congress may require documentary proof of citizenship — under Article I, Section 4 it plainly may, which is why the legislative track is the only one that has not been enjoined — but whether the verification problem is large enough to justify the verification cost, and that question has now been answered by courts, by Republican secretaries of state, and by the administration's own database, always in the same direction and always by roughly the same margin. The 'one-off' tell runs in both directions. Watch for supporters who cite a flagged number without saying what happened when it was investigated: the answer for Iowa was 277 of 2,176, for Denton County 47 of 84, and for the 278,000 nothing yet at all. And watch for opponents who cite 21.3 million without saying that the figure is a survey of self-reported document access rather than a count of votes lost, and without engaging the fact that the current federal safeguard is a signature the law forbids anyone to notarize. The facts that do not move whichever frame you prefer: the bill's text requires documentary proof at registration and photo ID at voting and reaches applications submitted after enactment; every completed audit puts noncitizen registration in the hundredths of a percent; Kansas's version blocked 31,089 eligible applicants; and the Senate has voted five times and does not have sixty.
pattern.unknowns: The pattern is context, not a thumb on the needle, which rests on this issue's checkable facts. That five verification efforts have produced small confirmed numbers is consistent with the problem being genuinely small and also consistent with existing detection methods being poor, and the record does not fully distinguish — no audit can find a noncitizen who never touches an immigration or DMV database. The Supreme Court's pending Arizona case could change the legal baseline for what states may require of the federal form, and would be decided after the November 2026 midterms. Whether a federally funded implementation with a working cure process would produce Kansas's 12.4 percent rejection rate or something far lower has never been tested, because no jurisdiction has tried it with money attached; the $10 billion in the House reconciliation framework would be the first such test and has not passed.

notAdjudicable: How to weigh one improperly cast vote against one wrongly prevented legitimate vote is a values question, not a factual one — the numbers on both sides of that ledger are now reasonably well measured, and people who agree on every number still disagree about the exchange rate.

Whether federal elections should be administered under national rules set by Congress or under fifty state systems is a constitutional-design preference, not an empirical question; the Elections Clause permits either, and both parties have argued both sides of it within the last five years.

Whether a verification requirement that nobody appears to be exploiting is nonetheless a defect worth fixing — the 'lock your door even in a safe neighborhood' intuition — is a question about acceptable risk and civic symbolism that no audit can settle.

Whether the legislative filibuster is a safeguard of minority rights or an anti-majoritarian obstruction is a values dispute about how a legislature should work, and it is currently being answered by both parties on the basis of what they want passed.

Whether the burden of proving eligibility should fall on the individual citizen or on the state is a foundational disagreement about the relationship between a person and their government, and it underlies almost every voting-rules fight in American history.
biasWatch: The bias running this argument is denominator blindness — each side quoting the numerator that suits it and refusing to state the number underneath. Supporters say '278,000 noncitizens registered' and do not say out of how many registrations, how many were confirmed rather than flagged, or what happened the last four times a number like that was investigated. Opponents say '21.3 million disenfranchised' and do not say that the figure is a survey of self-reported 'ready access' to a document, not a count of votes lost, applied to a requirement the statute limits to new applications. Both numbers are real and both are being used to mean something they do not mean. The concrete tell, and it works on every version of this argument: when someone gives you a number about voter fraud or voter suppression, ask what the denominator is and whether the number is a flag or a finding. If it is a flag, ask what the confirmation rate was — for Iowa it was 13 percent, for Denton County 56 percent of flags belonged to people who had already proved citizenship. If it is a survey, ask what the question actually asked. Then run the swap test on yourself. If you spent January 2022 arguing that a Senate procedural rule must not be allowed to block a federal election bill because democracy itself was at stake, you owe an account of why the rule is now sacred; and if you spent that month calling a federal election bill an illegitimate takeover of state authority, you owe one for why a national documentary-proof mandate on all fifty states is not. The thing the swap test cannot erase, whoever was in office: the current federal registration form asks you to swear you are a citizen and forbids anyone to make you prove it, and every place that has tried to make people prove it has caught a few dozen and turned away a few thousand. Both halves of that sentence are true, and any argument that only contains one of them is incomplete.
